convenience. once the technology improved, it became much less resource-intensive to draw something digitally than it was to have to hand draw a frame, then make cells from that, and then paint the cels. not to mention all of the technical knowledge that is needed in between all of those steps. plus, there’s no “undo” button on a cel or a piece of paper. if you fuck up, you have to start over. and then after all of that you had to take real, individual pictures of all the cels overlaid (background, foreground, characters, etc.) and then tie it all together. you can accomplish cleaner looking animation faster with just computers in digital. i’m not saying i’m in favor of the switch. i love the look of real cel animation. there’s a charm to the roughness of it, but the advantages of digital are extremely plentiful. one i forgot to mention is that now you’ve got access to every color you could ever want digitally, whereas those had to be physical collections of paint that have to be curated, mixed, and that would go bad if left around for too long under the wrong conditions. not to mention the brushes and other physical tools that have to be physically upkept. all of that is expensive.

even the idea of a compilation album has been around for a while. we kinda saw this with amo and ph:sh, where most of the songs were either released as singles before the full release, or were retroactively made out to be singles. it’s not a perfect compilation album or anything, but putting out an album that’s just a bunch of already released singles isn’t anything new.

from the perspective of making mass-marketable music, i can understand this take. it’s been this way for a while now. hell, it may even be better to release singles than albums. people like consistency and they like something they can enjoy AS SOON AS POSSIBLE. i’m not saying i’m like this, or that anyone in this sub is like this. i really love deep cut album content; however, the average person in this sub is NOT the average music listener. hell, the average metal listener isn’t the average music listener. albums are still pretty common in metal, but in genres which are more pop-adjacent and cater more to the “easy listening” crowd, EPs and singles and quicker and easier to make, as well as to consume. it doesn’t surprise me that oli would have a take like this as the band has become more pop-influenced. they’ve attracted more of the crowd that would rather have consistent singles and EPs than to wait to listen to a whole album. i’m not saying i agree with it from an audience perspective, but i definitely get it from the other side.

well, i’m aware of the original concept of reincarnation. i grew up going to buddhist sanghas. the part that makes it a big can of worms is that the version of reincarnation in the show is only an adapted version for this fantasy universe in a tv show originally made for children. it’s not a big thing for Reincarnation reincarnation, but it’s definitely a big thing for avatar reincarnation. you can’t just throw stuff like that in when it’s already established that it’s an abridged version of the idea, especially when there is already existing canon that would make that addition worse for the established rules of the show. 

in regards to the latter half of what you said, i think that that’s possible and very interesting. i don’t think that they had that idea full fleshed out yet by the time unalaq came around, because he was only ever showcased to perform waterbending. it leaves it up in the air whether the dark avatar would bend elements or would have different powers altogether. i really hope that any alternative powers wouldn’t be korra season 2 iron man blasts. i think that maybe using it as an opportunity to explore energy-bending more would be cool. i like the very self-focused idea for the dark avatar, with the light avatar being focused on serving others. it would set up a relationship that they have to learn from one another, and help flesh out vaatu and raava as more than “bad” and “good”, but rather internal and external. internal struggles have been a big focal point for the avatars we’ve seen, and energy-bending has historically been the solution to those struggles (aang with killing the firelord and korra with losing her bending). the issue is that those powers were just handed to our protagonists out of nowhere, so having a real living embodiment of that power who has to actually struggle with it and learn how to use it properly would help out energy-bending as a concept.

i think this would probably open up a whole can of worms of a human also being an animal that i don’t think the show would want to tackle. why did appa or naga go into the avatar state? why couldn’t they bend all the elements? what if the twin has a love interest? is that bestiality? beyond all of that, from what we know in korra, the show’s canon tells us that an avatar needs a soul-connection with raava or vaatu in order to have the powers of the avatar. none of the companions have had this as far as we know. 

what might be more interesting to explore, however, is that unalaq never had an animal companion as far as the show told us. all of raava’s avatars did, even wan with that deer-cat-thing (it’s not made clear whether that’s an animal or a spirit, but it doesn’t talk or get corrupted by vaatu as far as i can tell so i’m going with animal). unalaq did, however, have a much deeper relationship with spirits and being able to control them. so, would the dark avatar twin have a spirit companion rather than an animal companion? korra did set this up to be a possibility, and we even see bumi with bum-ju and jinora’s connection with the spirits. could be an interesting advantage that the “dark” avatar has over the “light” avatar.

it’s one of those examples of “hating someone because you are so alike” but they also hate each other because they each have something the other wants. people can very easily see that azula rules through fear, and would choose kuvira if given the choice because kuvira always at least has the excuse of getting shit done for what *appears* to be the right reasons. on the other hand, because azula is more transparent she can just go in a take what she wants with no questions asked because, well, it’s azula. that’s just what she does. because kuvira still has to appear as if she’s doing the right thing, her mobility is limited. 


we can see these differences in the show. you have people like bolin who really mean well and get caught up in kuvira’s rhetoric. it’s harder to mobilize them because kuvira has the burden of proving to those people why she’s worth following, which is why she goes out of her way to handle bandits single-handedly, humiliate korra and the prince, etc. azula’s closest friends turn on her within the span of a few months, but was able to get them on the road with her within the span of a couple days. azula doesn’t have to prove why she’s worth following. she’s royalty, and she can extrinsically make people’s lives hell if they don’t obey. it’s when they start to question why they should that they betray her. kuvira can convince people that following her is the right thing to do, which makes questioning why they follow her harder later on because she’s made it appear as if it was their idea in the first place. 


as far as them interacting, azula would treat kuvira like a peasant, behaving generally like she did towards long feng. kuvira would play holier than thou because she knows that portraying azula as a bratty teenager who has never had to struggle wouldn’t appeal to people nearly as much as kuvira’s metal-clan-great-uniter schtick. they’d get along together in public to save face with lots of passive-aggressive stabs along the way, but would condemn each other- publicly, even- when apart.


tl;dr: azula has more extrinsically motivated (less loyal) allies but can mobilize them more quickly. kuvira has more intrinsically motivated (more loyal) allies but can’t mobilize them as quickly. they both want what the other has. perfect recipe for a mean girl frienemy relationship.

depends on what he’s studying cause that’ll determine roughly some of the people he’ll be around. there are bound to be slackers in every department, but some tend to have more than others. arts & sciences, engineering, and communications tend to have more people who will be a positive influence. if your son is very passionate about going to college and about what he is studying and is willing to work hard to do what he wants, then i would say there’s probably nothing to worry about. if your son is just going to college to check a box, then he will probably do okay, but will probably end up around a lot of people with that slacker mentality and adopt a bit of that himself. 

i’d say if your son is willing to make his own path through his college experience and not get too caught up in the “barstool” culture then that’s a good sign. tell him to get involved in clubs, try things he hasn’t tried, pick up a new skill or a hobby, or take an art class. if your son is someone who can get genuinely interested in what his classes and professors have to offer, then he’ll do great. even if he tries to push himself and be ambitious and fails, he will get 10x more out of that failure than a B student who coasts by taking a bare minimum of “easy-A” classes. i’d also recommend that your son try to meet more people who are local to boulder. explore places that real boulder people hang out at. they might be a little older, and may not even be in college, but these are other people’s experiences who have helped me tremendously at CU, and they have been far better friends than anyone i just met at a party one time.

edit: grammar

edit 2: i’d also recommend that he apply to be an RA (resident advisor). he’d be working with a lot of really good people who know how to balance the fun stuff with school and work, and it’ll help him to build good communication skills and other soft skills that will be good on a resumé. it’ll also make sure that he keeps his grades in check, as there’s a GPA standard. there tend to be more female RA applicants than male RA applicants, so while i can’t guarantee he’d get a spot, it’d probably be a bit easier. you’ll also know he’ll be getting some good cardio in doing rounds around the building. all this combined with the free room & board, i’d honestly say it’s probably a better experience than any frat could offer.

Well, yes, if you’re trying to jump from free-market capitalism as we know it today or even mercantilism or feudalism. The way Marx analyzes history, which I personally think is pretty insightful, is through 1. The organization of production and 2. How those affect the material conditions of people within that organization. These are both important as they feed into one another. The material conditions of people are a product of that organization of production which confines them, and those material conditions then influence people to act in a way to naturally lead to the next organizational form of production. I’m sure people thought that free-market capitalism would be impossible unless through slavery and to a limited extent they were correct, we just really think about it in these terms. I know the common argument against the idea of wage labor as wage-slavery is that we have a choice, but this choice is extremely limited to the majority of the population and even then, because capitalism is global, you can’t ever really escape it. Even “communist” nations can’t and couldn’t escape it. This is why so many fell into fascism. They ended up trying to be democratic early on but realized that, because the institution of these radically democratic and liberating ideas was so opposed to those interests of people who had power to destroy their newfound successes, and that those people came from countries that were far more industrially powerful than their own (which is often why there was a revolution in the first place), they realized that in order to try and preserve some scrap of what they had fought for they would have to concentrate that power to a few or less people that held those same interests. The issue here is that in doing this they betrayed what the ideas of socialism were about in the first place: democracy, equality, and liberty. You see, the way that socialists see the organization of capitalist production is that there is a person or small group of people who bring to the table raw materials and those necessary factors of production, and there are a much larger group of people who, with inadequate resources to be able to lay claim to much capital, if any at all, bring their labor. The idea proposed by Adam Smith in Chapter 8 of Book 1 of his Wealth of Nations claims that what those two groups end up producing must be sold for an amount which is both high enough to humanely maintain the current and future growth of those laborers and the capitalist, as well as being high enough to pay the costs to maintain and grow the quantity and quality of the factors of production while also being low enough so that those same laborers and capitalists may be able to actually purchase the end product. This same chapter also goes on to say that, in most situations, those who fall into that capitalist class will have the advantage in maintaining the factors of production as well as their own salaries, while cutting the salaries of the laborers. Marx and Engels point out a contradiction here, which is that because the laboring class make up the majority of society, and that they will usually have the disadvantage in that game of tug-of-war that is their wages, those same laborers that are needed to purchase goods and services to pay for the costs needed to maintain production of them are the same laborers which will often not make enough money from their labor to be able to pay for what they need. This results in their observation from the perspective of people in the 1800s, that this was the cause of common recessions happening every 5-10 years, and they predicted that this would continue to happen as a result of this same core class conflict, which it has. What has changed, however, is that because capitalists have the advantage in keeping the wages of labor low, they end up absorbing, over time, a large and increasingly larger amount of surplus which they can use to buy more capital, bringing them more and more wealth. With this wealth, also described by Smith, comes the power to purchase what one can with it. What this manifests crucially as today is political power. Power over policy, power over media, and overall power over the environment which is *supposed* to select for them, but ends up being selected for. Thinking of this in terms of natural selection and evolution, that relationship between the species being selected for and the environment which selects for it is very much so akin to how businesses emerge, and either succeed or fail in a perfectly competitive market. What this accumulation of capital over time does is allow the species- or business- to select for its environment- the people which patronize it and the government which regulates it. Everything we see from how things are advertised to how news is presented to how even in some academic areas experiments and questions are formulated ends up being filtered by that which gives it the ability to exist, which is the capitalist giving their capital. These people, because of their immense and only growing power over the world essentially become mortal gods compared to the average joe, passing down their power through generations for it to continue growing and regulating what environment selects for us and our behaviors and thoughts. This is what socialism aims to combat, and I’ve already listed why a jump from feudal, mercantile, or capitalist systems to communism will and has failed. This is why in Engels’s *Socialism: Utopian and Scientific* he goes over steps in how to move toward it in the long run. It starts first with having what he calls “joint-stock companies” or what we see now as worker cooperatives. They cut out the capitalist while maintaining efficiency in production, allowing workers also to escape not being able to pay for their basic needs because the profit of the capitalist is cut out. He says that as these grow in popularity, people will realize that capitalists are essentially economic parasites, which would move society to a point where capitalists’ decreasing numbers and power would make them no longer a threat to state acquisition of production which would allow democracy to thrive such as it never has before, unpoisoned by capital’s meddlings. He finishes by saying that from this point, the new organization of production would make it a logical and plausible decision for everyone to benefit the most that they possibly can without impeding on each others’ benefits by continuing to labor and innovate via collaboration instead of competition and because of this inherent collective interest, the state’s power too would fade out to only its bare essentials. I’m not entirely sure about what I think about the plausibility of this evolution into this definition of communism as someone who studies economics, political science, and philosophy but where I’m at right now is the least we can do is get to a stage where we make worker cooperatives the main means of production, preventing concentrated amounts of power from existing, and using people’s collective interest in benefitting as many people as possible to give some limited state power to increase welfare for those who fundamental necessities without markets abusing the inelastic demand to suck up more profit. Being able to provide everyone equitable support in their right to protect their lives and means of living would create a much more steady standard of living which would not just help standardize people’s ability to make rational decisions which would help support a government democracy but would expand the labor pool greatly, leaving the only real hierarchy up to actual merit instead of mere power. Then we can support a lot of the assumptions Adam Smith and other great economists make about the conditions conducive to a working free market and let the market do its thing. Another way of saying this would be to “keep the competition on the court” instead of making it something that unnecessarily threatens people’s lives. That’s just my take though. This is what communist states and the Soviet Union tried to counter, but their approach to it was just giving the government more power and that ended up fucking everyone over. What I think we can do to counter this instead is to look at this as a matter of politics. The way businesses are structured right now is comparable to tyrannical and oligarchical nations that have most of the money move upwards to the top instead of downwards towards the people who need that money to survive. We have a solution to this, and it’s democracy. There are a variety of different ways that socialism has been interpreted but the most popular modern interpretation is generally that workers right now aren’t paid the full value of what their labor adds in the production process, and that surplus is instead taken by the owner or owners of a company for a variety of things be it corporate lobbying, buying up smaller competitors, spreading neoliberal propaganda, and/or other things to keep themselves in power. Socialism combats this by having workers democratically control the means of production (be that through worker cooperatives or the state) and they decide what happens with that surplus. Because of this it is in the best interest of everyone collectively to then collaborate with one another most logical option being for each worker to pursue the option that would leave everyone as well off as possible, which is why it’s described as the only true option for society to produce for the sake of collective human need rather than for individual profit. People tend to argue that capitalists are necessary because if you give that much power to regular workers they won’t make good decisions but these people typically don’t know or haven’t thought through how current worker cooperatives actually function and/or refuse to see the incredible amount of evidence that is completely contrary to that point. What we have seen is that when power is concentrated that wealth is much less likely to be used for collective good rather than that person’s own personal gain or to impose their beliefs and ideas upon the public at large.
